items.title: Howard Mandel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003
items.q: But on a jazz record, you’re reading Ira Gitler or Dan Morgenstern or Nat Hentoff, you’ve learned something about how the music was put together and who these people were. And it really helped me to figure out what jazz writing was about

ctx.x: Wow that’s unfortunate. And it’s so true, because I did the same thing. You obviously can’t hear the record when you’re holding it, but you can read about it. And that’s where I got a lot of my information, because there wasn’t all the publications out back then, and it’s a real art to writing good liner notes too.

It was an art and I think it really influenced my writing. That’s the nice thing. I mean liner notes were not — on rock records are very seldom any liner notes. If there were they were very jivey and hyped up. But on a jazz record, you’re reading Ira Gitler or Dan Morgenstern or Nat Hentoff, you’ve learned something about how the music was put together and who these people were. And it really helped me to figure out what jazz writing was about, more than the classic books that were available in the sixties,…
